subject: World War I
overview: From 1914 to 1918 the Allies (chiefly France, Britain, Russia, later Italy and the United States) fought the Central Powers (Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria). The fighting ran from the trenches of Belgium and France to the Eastern Front, the Alps, the Middle East and the open sea. Machine guns, artillery and poison gas made it deadlier than any war before it, with estimates commonly ranging from about 15 to 22 million military and civilian deaths. It ended with the defeat of the Central Powers in November 1918, and by then the German, Austro-Hungarian, Ottoman and Russian empires had all collapsed or were collapsing.

key_moments.title: Shots in Sarajevo
key_moments.text: On a state visit to Sarajevo, **Archduke Franz Ferdinand**, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and his wife Sophie were shot dead by **Gavrilo Princip**, a young Bosnian Serb nationalist. Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia, and a month of ultimatums and mobilisations, the **July Crisis**, pulled in the great powers through their alliances: Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on **28 July 1914**, and within days Germany, Russia, France and Britain were at war too. Princip was 19, too young under Austro-Hungarian law to be executed, so he was sentenced to 20 years in prison, where he died of tuberculosis in 1918, months before the war he had set off came to an end.
claims: Gavrilo Princip assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914.
Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July 1914.
Gavrilo Princip was too young to receive the death penalty under Austro-Hungarian law and was sentenced to 20 years in prison.
Gavrilo Princip died of tuberculosis in prison in 1918.

key_moments.title: The Marne halts Germany's advance
key_moments.text: Germany's war plan was to knock France out in a few weeks by swinging through Belgium, then turn east to face Russia. By early September German armies were close to Paris, but at the **First Battle of the Marne** French and British forces counter-attacked and drove them back. To rush reinforcements to the front, the French army commandeered **Paris taxicabs** to carry soldiers. The quick victory both sides had expected was gone: after a series of attempts to outflank each other, the armies dug in, and soon a line of **trenches** stretched from the North Sea coast to the Swiss border.
claims: The First Battle of the Marne took place in September 1914.
At the First Battle of the Marne, French and British forces stopped the German advance on Paris and forced the German armies to retreat.
The French army used Paris taxicabs to carry soldiers to the front during the First Battle of the Marne.
After the First Battle of the Marne, the Western Front settled into a line of trenches from the North Sea to the Swiss border.

key_moments.title: Verdun, the Somme and the first tanks
key_moments.text: 1916 brought the war's longest battles on the Western Front. At **Verdun**, German and French armies fought for most of the year over a ring of forts, at the cost of hundreds of thousands of casualties. On **1 July 1916** British and French troops attacked along the **Somme**, and the British army suffered about 57,000 casualties on that single day, nearly 20,000 of them killed, its worst day in history. The Somme also saw a new weapon: on **15 September 1916**, at Flers–Courcelette, the British sent **tanks** into battle for the first time, armoured machines meant to cross the barbed wire and trenches that had stopped infantry for two years.
claims: The Battle of Verdun between German and French forces lasted for most of 1916.
The Battle of the Somme began on 1 July 1916.
The British army suffered about 57,000 casualties, including nearly 20,000 dead, on the first day of the Battle of the Somme, the worst day in its history.
Tanks were used in battle for the first time by the British at Flers–Courcelette on 15 September 1916, during the Battle of the Somme.

key_moments.title: America enters, Russia leaves, Germany yields
key_moments.text: Angered by Germany's **unrestricted submarine warfare** and the Zimmermann Telegram, the **United States** declared war on Germany in April 1917. In the east, revolution toppled Tsar Nicholas II, and the new Bolshevik government made peace with Germany at **Brest-Litovsk** in March 1918. Freed to shift troops west, Germany launched its **Spring Offensive** in 1918 and came close to a breakthrough, but the Allies, now joined by fresh American troops, answered with the **Hundred Days Offensive**. Germany signed the **Armistice** in Marshal Ferdinand Foch's railway carriage in the Forest of Compiègne, and the guns fell silent at 11 a.m. on **11 November 1918**. In June 1940, Adolf Hitler had the same carriage brought back to the same spot for France's surrender.
claims: The United States declared war on Germany in April 1917.
Soviet Russia signed the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk with the Central Powers in March 1918.
The Armistice of 11 November 1918 was signed in Ferdinand Foch's railway carriage in the Forest of Compiègne and took effect at 11 a.m.
In June 1940, Adolf Hitler had the French sign their armistice in the same railway carriage at Compiègne.

deep_facts.text: In January 1917 German Foreign Secretary Arthur Zimmermann sent a coded telegram offering Mexico an alliance if the United States entered the war, with the promise that Mexico could recover Texas, New Mexico and Arizona. British codebreakers in Room 40 intercepted and decoded it, and its publication in American newspapers caused an uproar. Many Americans suspected a British forgery, and Germany could simply have denied it. Instead, Zimmermann publicly admitted that the telegram was genuine.
claims: In January 1917 Arthur Zimmermann sent a telegram proposing a German alliance with Mexico if the United States entered the war.
The Zimmermann Telegram promised that Mexico could recover Texas, New Mexico and Arizona.
British codebreakers in Room 40 intercepted and decoded the Zimmermann Telegram.
Arthur Zimmermann publicly confirmed that the telegram was genuine.

deep_facts.text: The word "tank" began as a cover story. While the British were secretly building their first armoured fighting vehicles, workers and officials were told the large steel hulls were water tanks or water carriers, so that anyone who saw them would not guess what they were for. The nickname stuck, and a war machine still carries the name of a water container.
claims: The British called their first armoured fighting vehicles "tanks" to keep them secret during development.
The name "tank" was chosen to suggest that the vehicles were water tanks or water carriers.

deep_facts.text: The Armistice was signed around 5 a.m. on 11 November 1918, but it did not take effect until 11 a.m., and fighting went on through the final hours. At 10:59 a.m., one minute before the ceasefire, American soldier Henry Gunther charged a German machine-gun position and was shot dead. He is generally recognised as the last soldier killed in action in the war.
claims: The Armistice of 11 November 1918 was signed early in the morning and took effect at 11 a.m.
Henry Gunther, an American soldier, was killed at 10:59 a.m. on 11 November 1918.
Henry Gunther is generally recognised as the last soldier killed in action in World War I.

connections.name: Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria
connections.connection: His assassination in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 set off the July Crisis that led to the war.

connections.name: Gavrilo Princip
connections.connection: The Bosnian Serb student who shot Franz Ferdinand and Sophie in Sarajevo.

connections.name: Wilhelm II
connections.connection: German Emperor throughout the war, who abdicated and fled to the Netherlands in November 1918.

connections.name: Woodrow Wilson
connections.connection: US President who took the United States into the war in April 1917 and set out his Fourteen Points for the peace.

connections.name: Georges Clemenceau
connections.connection: French Prime Minister from 1917 who led France to victory and pressed for harsh terms on Germany at the peace conference.

connections.name: Ferdinand Foch
connections.connection: Supreme Allied Commander in 1918, in whose railway carriage the Armistice was signed.

connections.name: Paul von Hindenburg
connections.connection: German commander who won at Tannenberg in 1914 and later directed Germany's war effort as Chief of the General Staff.

connections.name: Erich Ludendorff
connections.connection: Hindenburg's chief partner in command, who planned Germany's 1918 Spring Offensive.

connections.name: Nicholas II of Russia
connections.connection: Russian Tsar whose empire's wartime collapse forced his abdication in March 1917.

connections.name: Treaty of Versailles
connections.connection: The 1919 peace treaty with Germany that formally ended the war between Germany and the Allies.

connections.name: Russian Revolution
connections.connection: Grew out of Russia's wartime losses and led the Bolsheviks to take Russia out of the war in 1918.

connections.name: Battle of the Somme
connections.connection: The 1916 Anglo-French offensive that saw Britain's worst day of losses and the first use of tanks.

connections.name: Battle of Verdun
connections.connection: The longest battle of the war, fought between French and German armies through most of 1916.

connections.name: World War II
connections.connection: Grew in part out of the grievances and unresolved disputes left by the First World War and its peace settlement.
